source_text:
Fragmenta in epistulam ad Titum (in catenis)
Tit 1,12®13a Ἐπειδὴ ὁ ποιητὴς ὁ εἰρηκὼς τὸ Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία,
γαστέρες ἀργαί, ἐπιλαμβανόμενος αὐτῶν εἶπεν ὡς κακῶς δεικνύντων τάφον ∆ιὸς
τὸν οὐκ ὄντα, ἐχρήσατο δὲ τῷ αὐτῷ στίχῳ Παῦλος, ἴνα μὴ νομισθῇ τῷ ποιητῇ
συντρέχειν καὶ τῷ λεγομένῳ ∆ιῒ μαρτυρεῖν ἀθανασίαν, ἐπήγαγεν· ἡ μαρτυρία αὕτη
ἀληθής ἐστιν. ἐκεῖνος ἐψεύσατο τῷ ∆ιῒ συνηγορῶν, ἐγὼ δὲ ἀληθεύω λέγων ὅτι οἱ
Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσταί εἰσιν καὶ γαστέρες ἀργαί. αὕτη ἡ μαρτυρία ἀληθής, οὐκ ἐκείνη.
thought_title: Paul limits his use of the poet's line to the true charge about Cretans
orientation: Severianus opens the fragments by explaining why Paul, after quoting the Cretan poet's saying about Cretans, adds that this testimony is true.
pass_a_gloss: Since the poet who said 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle gluttons,' seizing on them said that they wrongly point to a tomb of Zeus that does not exist, and Paul used the same verse, so that he might not be thought to run together with the poet and to testify immortality to the so-called Zeus, he added: 'this testimony is true.' That one lied defending Zeus, but I speak truth saying that the Cretans are always liars and idle gluttons. This testimony is true, not that one.

lemmas.gloss: to run together with, agree with

choices.why: The verb means to lay hold of or attack; 'seizing on' keeps the aggressive force of the poet's criticism of the Cretans.
The phrase denies the reality of Zeus's tomb; 'that does not exist' preserves the ontological negation.
The verb suggests moving in the same direction or agreeing; 'run together with' keeps the metaphor of alignment.
The participle λεγομένῳ distances Paul from affirming Zeus's reality; 'so-called' marks this distancing.
The dative Διῒ with συνηγορῶν means speaking in Zeus's defense; 'defending Zeus' captures the support, and 'lied' keeps the contrast with Paul's truth-telling.
rejected: That one lied as an advocate for Zeus
That one spoke falsely pleading for Zeus

bible_refs.note: Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία, γαστέρες ἀργαί

pass_b_english: The poet who said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle gluttons” (Titus 1:12) was attacking them for pointing to a tomb of Zeus that does not exist. Paul used that same line, but so that he would not be thought to agree with the poet and testify to the immortality of the so-called Zeus, he added, “This testimony is true” (Titus 1:13). This poet lied in defending Zeus, but Paul in effect says, “I speak the truth when I say that Cretans are always liars and idle gluttons.” This testimony is true, not that one.

last_rejected.quote: but I speak the truth when I say that Cretans are always liars and idle gluttons
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐγὼ δὲ ἀληθεύω λέγων ὅτι οἱ Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσταί εἰσιν καὶ γαστέρες ἀργαί
last_rejected.why: Source has Paul speaking ('ἐγὼ δέ' = 'but I'), but English 'I' is ambiguous—could be author or Paul. The voices brief marks Paul as quoted Scripture in sections including u01-open. The English should clarify this is Paul's voice, not Severianus's.
last_rejected.fix: but Paul speaks the truth when he says that Cretans are always liars and idle gluttons
last_rejected.ruling: ἐγὼ δέ naturally renders 'but I'; context makes Paul the speaker clear. Ambiguity claim is stylistic preference, not meaning change.

problems.quote: That poet lied in defending Zeus, but I speak the truth
problems.why: Sudden first person 'I' after third person about Paul; is this Severianus or Paul speaking?
problems.fix: Identify speaker: Paul (or Severianus speaking as Paul)

problems.quote: but I speak the truth when I say that Cretans are always liars
problems.why: Sudden first person 'I'—is this Paul speaking, Severianus, or the poet? Unclear after third-person framing.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'Paul in effect says, I speak the truth…'
